metadata.reasoning: web-grounded narrative-person adjudication using the PERSON_METHODOLOGY.md label definitions and source hierarchy

records.author: Elin Hilderbrand
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: Independent structural descriptions identify a third-person narrative voice that moves among characters, including Vivi and a Nantucket chapter. Changing focal characters does not introduce a first- or second-person narrating strand.
records.ambiguity: The novel uses many focal perspectives and a personified-Nantucket chapter, but the available sources characterize the controlling narration as third person.

sources.title: Golden Girl Chapters 1-10 Summary & Analysis
sources.supports: Explicitly identifies the novel's third-person narrative voice and says it follows Vivi and other figures.

sources.title: Golden Girl by Elin Hilderbrand
sources.supports: Explicitly describes third-person POV and frequent shifts among character perspectives.

records.author: John Grisham
records.label: FIRST
records.evidence_summary: The publisher's opening excerpt has Luke's first-person possessives in continuous scene narration and identifies Luke Chandler as narrator; an independent study source also calls Luke the first-person narrator.
records.ambiguity: None material; the primary excerpt directly establishes Luke's narrating I-voice.

sources.title: A Painted House — John Grisham
sources.supports: Supplies the opening excerpt (including Luke's first-person reference) and identifies Luke Chandler as narrator.

sources.title: A Painted House
sources.supports: Explicitly calls Luke Chandler the first-person narrator.

records.author: Frances Parkinson Keyes
records.label: UNRESOLVED
records.evidence_summary: The located contemporary review and catalog/review descriptions establish a multi-character mystery but do not explicitly state narration person or provide sustained readable narrative text. That is not enough to infer a book-level narrator.
records.ambiguity: Character-centered plot descriptions are compatible with either a first-person participant recounting events or third-person narration; no diagnostic primary excerpt was found.
records.searched_but_not_found: Exact-title searches for 'narrator', 'point of view', 'Chapter I', Google Books, library/Open Library previews, scholarship, and contemporary reviews found bibliographic and plot material only; no lawful preview or credible explicit POV statement was located.

sources.title: THE ROYAL BOX
sources.supports: Establishes the book's multi-character mystery structure, but does not establish grammatical narrative person.

sources.title: The Royal Box by Frances Parkinson Keyes
sources.supports: Corroborates the named cast and murder premise, but provides no reliable explicit POV description.

records.author: John Hersey
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: A contemporary serialized text excerpt narrates Joppolo externally in third person; an independent literary source additionally identifies an omniscient narrator focused on Joppolo. This is a third-person structure, not a participating narrator.
records.ambiguity: The narrative is focalized around Joppolo, but both sources distinguish that focus from the omniscient narrator.

sources.title: John Hersey Writing Styles in A Bell for Adano
sources.supports: Explicitly calls the narrator omniscient and explains its focus on Joppolo.

sources.title: A Bell for Adano — syndicated chapter excerpt
sources.supports: Provides direct text with Major Joppolo and Little Zito represented externally in scene narration.

records.author: Stephen King
records.label: FIRST
records.evidence_summary: The publisher provides an opening extract; independent structural analysis identifies named narrator/then-now chapters, with Sandy as the principal storyteller and other officers supplying their accounts. A separate independent review explicitly identifies the book as first person with multiple points of view. Multiple autonomous narrators remain FIRST because the documented strands are first-person accounts, rather than different grammatical persons.
records.ambiguity: The framing and flashbacks can make the narrator shifts feel layered, but sources consistently identify the voices as first-person accounts rather than a first/third alternation.

sources.title: From a Buick 8 by Stephen King
sources.supports: Provides the official opening extract and establishes the present-day Ned/Troop D frame.

sources.title: Ghost story techniques in 'From a Buick 8'
sources.supports: Describes named narrator and then/now chapter titles, Sandy as main narrator, and other officers' accounts.

sources.title: Talk Stephen King: From A Buick 8 Journal #1
sources.supports: Explicitly says the book is told in first person with multiple points of view.

records.author: Nicholas Sparks
records.label: ALTERNATING
records.evidence_summary: The author's official excerpt narrates present-day Maggie externally in third person. An independent chapter analysis identifies the sustained Ocracoke flashback as Maggie's first-person telling to Mark. These are autonomous present and retrospective narrative strands in different grammatical persons.
records.ambiguity: The first-person strand is framed as Maggie's story to Mark, but it is the novel's sustained flashback structure rather than an isolated document.

sources.title: The Wish Character Analysis
sources.supports: States that Maggie tells the story and recounts the 1995 events to Mark.

sources.title: The Wish excerpt
sources.supports: Provides sustained present-day third-person narration centered on Maggie.

sources.title: The Wish Chapters 1-3 Summary & Analysis
sources.supports: Explicitly identifies the Ocracoke flashback as Maggie's first-person embedded narrative to Mark.

records.author: Nick Bantock
records.label: FIRST
records.evidence_summary: The entire narrative is presented as correspondence between Griffin and Sabine. The two autonomous epistolary voices are both first-person letter writers; they do not form an alternating mix of grammatical persons under this project's definition.
records.ambiguity: The book has two correspondents, but multiplicity of first-person writers is not ALTERNATING unless the strands use different persons.

sources.title: An Open Letter to Nick Bantock
sources.supports: Describes the work as an epistolary novel and says its entire narrative consists of nineteen pieces of mail.

sources.title: Special Delivery
sources.supports: Describes the physical letters and postcards exchanged between Griffin and Sabine.

records.author: Abby Jimenez
records.label: FIRST
records.evidence_summary: A publisher-affiliated extract opens in a speaker's first-person voice, and independent review sources establish that the novel has autonomous Samantha and Xavier POV chapters. Multiple first-person narrators retain the FIRST label because the persons do not differ across strands.
records.ambiguity: Available evidence exposes first-person grammar and dual POV but lacks a stable official full sample for both speakers, so confidence is moderate.

sources.title: Read an extract from Say You'll Remember Me by Abby Jimenez
sources.supports: Provides first-chapter text in a narrating I-voice, including the speaker's reference to 'our faces.'

sources.title: Reviews — Say You'll Remember Me
sources.supports: Independent reader review explicitly calls the book dual POV and identifies Samantha and Xavier.

sources.title: Say You'll Remember Me
sources.supports: A separate reader review explicitly labels the novel 'Dual point of view.'

records.author: Irving Wallace
records.label: UNRESOLVED
records.evidence_summary: Google Books and a university-hosted genre account establish Steve Randall as the central character and show searchable third-person vocabulary, but neither offers enough directly inspectable narrative text to meet the evidence floor. No reliable lawful sustained preview or explicit POV analysis was found.
records.ambiguity: Third-person plot summaries and character lists cannot distinguish external narration from a first-person narrator writing about Steve; abstention is required without diagnostic text.
records.searched_but_not_found: Exact-title searches for 'narrator', 'point of view', 'first person', 'third person', chapter opening, Google Books queries, library/OverDrive samples, scholarship, and contemporary reviews found descriptions and metadata but no lawful sustained narrative preview or explicit credible POV classification.

sources.title: 1972 The Word
sources.supports: Identifies Steve Randall as the novel's hero and outlines its multiple characters and plot, but does not explicitly establish grammar.

sources.title: The Word
sources.supports: Provides bibliographic confirmation and searchable-text terms, but no sustained inspectable narrative excerpt.

records.author: John Grisham
records.label: THIRD
records.evidence_summary: An official publisher-authorized excerpt presents Kyle McAvoy externally in dialogue and scene narration. The publisher description likewise consistently refers to Kyle in the third person; no competing narrating voice is indicated.
records.ambiguity: None material; the authorized sample directly shows an external narrator.

sources.title: Extract from The Associate by John Grisham
sources.supports: Supplies the novel excerpt with Kyle represented externally in narration and dialogue attribution.

sources.title: The Associate by John Grisham
sources.supports: Official description consistently frames Kyle McAvoy as an externally narrated protagonist.
